title: One Life, Two Countries, Two Courts
summary: A person with property in more than one country does not have one estate in practice; each country's courts and rules reach the property within their power. Domicile, the location of each asset and the process called probate decide who gets what and how long it takes. Learn these three ideas before any lawyer drafts a will.
body:
When you own property in two countries, you effectively leave two estates, each handled by its own courts under its own rules. Planning a cross-border estate means making those two processes agree before anyone needs them.

Recall

Q. What do attribution rules do?

A. They tax income, and sometimes gains, from property transferred or lent to certain related people back to the person who made the transfer.

Q. Who holds legal title to trust property?

A. The trustee, who must manage it entirely for the beneficiaries under the deed and the duties the law imposes.

Q. What is a condition precedent in a contract?

A. An event or act that must happen before a party's obligation arises, such as a notice being given in time. Miss it, and the right may never come into existence.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer who works across borders accumulates property in more than one place: land, company shares, bank accounts, perhaps a home. Each piece sits under the power of a particular country's courts. If you die or lose capacity without a plan built for that fact, your family will meet several legal processes, in several languages of procedure, at the moment they can least manage it. This is concept teaching. Succession law differs sharply between countries and between provinces or states inside them, and nothing here is a conclusion about any place. LEX joins me because the answer often turns on which country's law applies, which is a legal question, not a family one. Professional sign-off required: an estates lawyer in each country where you hold property.

Domicile and the location of assets

Plain English first. Two facts drive a cross-border estate: where you belong, and where each thing you own is.

The professional framing. Domicile is, broadly, the country a person treats as their permanent home, the place they intend to return to and remain; it is a legal concept distinct from residence or citizenship, and in common law systems it can be hard to change. The situs of an asset is where the law treats that asset as located: land is located where it lies, a bank account usually where the branch is, and shares often where the company's register is kept, though rules differ. Many common law systems traditionally apply the law of the place where land lies to succession to that land, and the law of the person's domicile to most other property. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, because some systems apply one law to the whole estate, and some allow a person to choose.

Applied example, hypothetical. A developer domiciled in Country A owns a home and a bank account there, and a parcel of land and a company in Country B. When he dies, Country B's courts will likely apply their own rules to the land, and may require their own process before the land can be sold or transferred. Country A's rules may govern the home and the account. If his will was written for Country A and never thought about Country B, his family may find that the land passes under a different rule, to different people, or not at all until a court in Country B is satisfied.

Say that out loud now.

Probate: the court's permission to act

Plain English. When someone dies, their property does not instantly belong to anybody who can act on it. Someone must be given authority. Probate is the court process that confirms a will is valid and appoints the executor, giving that person legal authority to collect, manage and distribute the estate. Where there is no will, a similar process appoints an administrator.

For a cross-border estate, the critical fact is that one country's probate is not automatically recognised in another. Some countries, particularly within the Commonwealth, have procedures to recognise or reseal a grant made elsewhere; others require a fresh application, sometimes called ancillary probate. Each takes time, documents, translation and fees. While it is pending, the assets in that country may be frozen: a bank may refuse to release funds, a land registry may refuse to register a sale, a company may refuse to register a share transfer.

Second applied example, hypothetical. A developer dies holding 2,000,000 dollars in a Country B bank account and a project company in Country B with a construction loan. The loan agreement makes the death of the guarantor an event that the lender may treat as a default. The executor in Country A obtains probate in four months. Country B requires its own grant, which takes another nine months. For those nine months, nobody can sign for his shares or release the account. The lender, worried, reserves its rights. The project stalls not because anybody did anything wrong, but because the estate had no authority where the asset was.

Incapacity is the harder case

Death at least produces a clear trigger. Incapacity, through illness or injury, does not. If you cannot manage your affairs, someone needs legal authority to sign for you: a power of attorney, or a court-appointed guardian or similar. Powers of attorney are creatures of local law, and one made in Country A may not be accepted by a bank or registry in Country B. A developer who loses capacity mid-project without documents that work in each country can leave his companies unable to sign anything. That is why planning covers both events, and why we will spend time on incapacity this week.

How the best do it

Families with property in several countries who plan well usually keep three things current: a single written summary of every asset, its location, how it is held and which document governs it; a set of wills and incapacity documents, one set per country where needed, drafted to work together; and a named coordinator, often a lead lawyer, who knows where every document is and who to call. A small developer can copy all three with a spreadsheet, two lawyers and an annual review.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming one well-drafted will covers the world. The control is to list every asset by country, ask an estates lawyer in each country how that asset passes and what process will be needed, and build documents for each country that are coordinated with the others.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is confusing citizenship, residence for tax and domicile for succession. They are different tests, they can point to three different countries, and each affects a different question.

Callback

Two weeks ago, in the trusts lessons, we saw that property properly held in a trust often sits outside a person's own estate. That is one reason cross-border families use trusts and companies: an asset already owned by a trust or a company may not need probate in its country at all, because the owner did not die. The structure must be genuine for that to hold, which Rule 91 reminds us depends on real decisions in the right place.

Six-Lens Check

Tax. Each country may tax the estate, the transfer or the heirs differently, and some may tax the same property, so double tax relief must be checked. Liability. An executor can be personally liable for distributing before debts and taxes are settled. Banking. Accounts may freeze until local authority is shown, and loan agreements may treat death or incapacity as an event of default. Governance. Companies need a way to keep signing when an owner or director dies or loses capacity. Estate. Coordinated wills, by country, with incapacity documents that each country will accept. Exit. Heirs may need to sell; know what each country requires before a sale can close.

Recap

Domicile and situs decide which law applies to which asset. Probate gives someone authority to act, country by country. Incapacity needs authority too, and documents that work in each place. Plan each country, and coordinate them all.

Next lesson: Ford, on the estate of Howard Hughes, who died in 1976 with property, residence and a will all in dispute.
checklist: I list every asset I own by country, form of ownership and governing document.
I know my domicile, my tax residence and my citizenship, and that they are different tests.
I ask an estates lawyer in each country how my assets there would pass.
I know whether each country recognises a foreign grant of probate or needs its own.
I check which loans or agreements treat my death or incapacity as an event of default.
I have incapacity documents that a bank and registry in each country will accept.
I name a coordinator who knows where every document is.
I review the plan every year and after any move or major purchase.

Domicile is the country you treat as your permanent home, a legal test distinct from residence or citizenship. Many common law systems apply the law of the land's location to land and the law of domicile to most other property, but rules differ, so verify. terms: Domicile — the country a person treats as their permanent home, used in many legal systems to decide which law governs succession to most property.
Situs — the place where the law treats an asset as located, such as where land lies or where a bank account is held.
Probate — the court process that confirms a will and gives the executor legal authority to deal with the estate.

hostile.q: You personally guarantee this loan and you live in another country. If you die, who signs for you here, and how long will that take?
hostile.a: I have a will drafted for this country, coordinated with my home-country will, naming an executor who can apply here directly. My lawyer here estimates the local process and has the documents on file. Separately, the borrower company has a second authorised signatory, and my shares are held through a holding company, so the company keeps operating while the estate is administered. I will give you the timeline in writing.

title: Howard Hughes: The Estate With No Will and Three Homes
summary: Howard Hughes died in 1976 without a valid will anyone could find, after years living in hotels in several countries. Purported wills surfaced, one was rejected by a Nevada jury in 1978, and states contested where he had been domiciled. Seven forensic steps show how an unplanned, multi-place life became years of litigation.
body:
Howard Hughes, one of the richest people of his time, died in April 1976 without a will that anyone could prove. His estate became a long contest over which will was real, who his heirs were, and which state could tax him, because nobody had settled where he lived or what he wanted.

Recall

Q. What are domicile and situs?

A. Domicile is the country a person treats as their permanent home. Situs is where the law treats an asset as located. Together they often decide which law governs each asset on death.

Q. What is a fixed trust?

A. A trust whose deed sets each beneficiary's share, leaving the trustee no choice about who benefits.

Q. What is a time bar in a construction contract?

A. A clause that removes a party's right to a claim if notice is not given within a stated period.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a real case, and I give only facts I am confident of. I leave out figures, because published estimates of the estate's value vary. Read a reliable history before relying on any detail. Cole assists because the failure is fundamentally about missing evidence: the evidence of intention, of home and of authority that a plan would have created. Hughes was an extreme case, but the pattern is ordinary. Any person who lives and owns property in more than one place, and does not plan, gives several courts something to decide.

1. Timeline

Hughes was born in Texas and built a business empire in aviation, film and later Nevada property and casinos. In his last years he lived in seclusion in hotels in several countries, surrounded by a small group of aides. He died on 5 April 1976 on a flight bound for Houston. No valid will was found among his papers, despite reports over the years that he had made one. Within weeks, purported wills began to appear. The best known, the so-called "Mormon will", surfaced at the headquarters of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Salt Lake City and named, among many others, a Utah service-station operator named Melvin Dummar. In 1978 a jury in Nevada found that document was not a valid will. In the absence of a will, the estate passed under intestacy rules to relatives, after years of proceedings to establish who they were. Separately, Texas and California each claimed he had been domiciled in their state, which mattered for death taxes, and the dispute reached the United States Supreme Court before it was resolved. Verify these dates and details against a reliable source before you rely on them.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choices were omissions. Not leaving a will that could be found and proved. Not documenting where he regarded as home. And, in his final years, leaving the practical management of his affairs to aides, with no transparent, legally robust arrangement for incapacity or succession.

3. Assumptions

The working assumption, as far as one can infer, was that there would be time later, or that his organisation would handle it. A second assumption, common among powerful people, is that control while alive translates into control after death. It does not. After death, control passes to whoever the law says, and the law says it through courts.

4. Incentives

Once he died without a proved will, every incentive pointed toward litigation. Each potential heir had reason to argue for a reading that favoured them. Anyone holding a purported will had reason to press it. Each state with a plausible claim to his domicile had reason to argue that he lived there, because domicile carried the right to tax. None of those parties was doing anything unusual. The absence of a plan created a prize, and prizes attract claimants.

Say that out loud now.

5. Warning signs ignored

Cole's list. A person of enormous wealth with no publicly confirmed, current will. A life spent moving between hotels in different countries, with no clear record of a permanent home. Isolation, and reliance on a small circle of aides, which leaves any later document open to questions about capacity and influence. And business interests spread across several states. Each is a sign that the estate would become a legal contest; together they made that close to certain.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment of death without a provable will and without settled evidence of domicile. Before it, any of those gaps could have been closed in an afternoon with lawyers. After it, they could only be argued.

7. Root cause

The root cause was not complexity. Complex estates are settled quietly every year. It was the absence of three ordinary documents and one ordinary record: a valid, findable will, coordinated with any property elsewhere; incapacity arrangements; and written evidence of where he regarded as his permanent home.

The ordinary-person version

This is a composite example, hypothetical, to bring the case down to your scale. A developer domiciled in Country A owns a home in Country A, two rental condominiums in Country B and shares in a Country B project company. He has a will made in Country A twenty years ago, which predates the Country B assets. He spends half of each year in each country. He dies. His children find the old will. Lawyers in Country B ask which country he was domiciled in; the answer affects which law applies to his shares. His second spouse, from Country B, argues he had settled there. The condominiums need local probate. The project lender reserves its rights. None of this is exotic. Each step costs months and fees, and the family relationships pay too.

A second worked example of cost, hypothetical. Suppose a dispute over domicile and a contested will takes four years to resolve, with combined legal costs of 600,000 dollars, and that during those years a 3,000,000 dollar property portfolio cannot be refinanced or sold and loses 2 percent of value a year to deferred maintenance and missed opportunities. The portfolio loss is about 3,000,000 multiplied by one minus 0.98 to the 4th, which is one minus 0.922, giving about 234,000 dollars. Total leakage is about 834,000 dollars, against a planning cost of perhaps 20,000 dollars for coordinated documents.

Cole's three records

Cole reduces the case to three records every person with property in two places should be able to hand over within a day: the current wills and where the originals are; a short signed note of where they regard as home and why; and the incapacity documents for each country. If any of the three cannot be produced, the estate is already on its way to becoming an argument. Producing them is an afternoon's work with lawyers. Arguing about them, as the Hughes estate showed, can take years.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is postponement. Every successful person believes there will be time. The control is a deadline: wills, incapacity documents and a domicile note done before your next major cross-border purchase, and reviewed every year after.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is keeping the will secret and the asset list in your head. A will nobody can find is no will. Professional sign-off required: an estates lawyer in each country where you hold property.

Callback

In the records week, Vera taught that a record made at the time is evidence and a later recollection is argument. Hughes's estate was years of argument about facts, his home and his wishes, that a few records made in his lifetime would have settled.

Recap

Hughes died in 1976 with no proved will and a contested domicile. Purported wills failed, heirs had to be established, and states fought over the right to tax. The root cause was missing documents and missing evidence.

Rule 92: Never let your estate depend on what a court decides you intended; record where you consider home, keep a valid will for each country where you hold property, coordinated with the others and findable by the people who need it, and put incapacity documents in place that each country will accept.

Next lesson: Roman, on the money a cross-border estate loses, and how to keep it liquid.
checklist: I have a valid will that covers every country where I hold property.
My wills are coordinated so one does not revoke or contradict another.
My executor and coordinator know where every original document is kept.
I have written down where I regard as my permanent home and why.
I have incapacity documents accepted in each country where I hold assets.
I set a deadline for my estate documents before my next cross-border purchase.
I review my estate plan every year and after every move, marriage or major purchase.

Purported wills appeared, including the so-called Mormon will naming Melvin Dummar, which a Nevada jury found invalid in 1978. The estate passed under intestacy rules after years spent establishing his relatives, and Texas and California each claimed his domicile for death taxes, a dispute that reached the United States Supreme Court. The root cause was not complexity. It was the absence of a findable will, of incapacity arrangements, and of evidence of where he regarded as home. Once he died, every gap became a prize to litigate. terms: Intestacy — the situation of dying without a valid will, in which local law decides who inherits.
Executor — the person named in a will to collect, manage and distribute the estate under the court's authority.
Administrator — the person appointed by a court to administer an estate when there is no will or no executor able to act.

hostile.q: You own property in two countries and your will is ten years old. If you die tomorrow, how long before your heirs can sell the land here?
hostile.a: Today I cannot give you a confident answer, and that is the problem I am fixing. My lawyer here is drafting a will for my assets in this country, coordinated with my home will so neither revokes the other, and confirming what local process the executor will need and how long it usually takes. I will have it signed before closing, and I will give you a letter from my lawyer setting out the expected process.

title: The Money a Cross-Border Estate Loses
summary: When a developer dies or loses capacity with assets in two countries, value leaks through frozen accounts, probate costs, triggered loans, forced sales, currency spreads and tax collected twice. Each leak can be estimated, and most can be reduced. This lesson prices them and builds a liquidity plan.
body:
An unplanned cross-border estate rarely loses its value in one blow. It leaks, through months of frozen cash, loans that can be called, costs in two currencies and assets sold in a hurry, and a liquidity plan is how you stop the leaks.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 92?

A. Never let your estate depend on what a court decides you intended; record where you consider home, keep coordinated, findable wills for each country where you hold property, and have incapacity documents each country will accept.

Q. What is cost drag in a trust?

A. The gap between what assets earn and what beneficiaries receive after fees and costs, which compounds over time.

Q. What is an event of default in a loan?

A. A defined event, such as non-payment, a covenant breach or insolvency, that allows the lender to exercise remedies, including demanding repayment.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I look at estates the way a lender does: where does the cash come from, and what happens in the months nobody can sign? A developer's estate is usually asset-rich and cash-poor, full of land, company shares and guarantees. Death or incapacity is exactly when those assets are hardest to use. All figures below are hypothetical and round. Costs and taxes vary by country, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The six leaks

Plain English. Value leaves an unplanned estate through six holes.

  • Frozen liquidity. Accounts in the deceased's name may be inaccessible until local authority is shown.
  • Process costs. Legal, court, translation, valuation and executor costs, in each country.
  • Triggered debt. Loans and guarantees that treat death or incapacity as an event of default or a review trigger.
  • Forced sales. Assets sold quickly to pay tax or debt, at a discount to what patient selling would achieve.
  • Currency. Conversion costs and the risk of converting at a bad rate when funds must move between countries.
  • Double tax. Two countries taxing the same property or transfer, with relief that must be claimed and may be incomplete.

The professional framing is an estate liquidity gap: the difference between the cash the estate will need in its first 12 to 24 months and the cash it can actually reach in that time.

Pricing the leaks

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer dies with a gross estate of 20,000,000 dollars: a 2,000,000 dollar home in Country A, 1,500,000 dollars of cash split between the two countries, and 16,500,000 dollars of shares in project companies in Country B. Two project loans each require the lender's consent to a change of guarantor within 90 days of the guarantor's death.

The estate needs, in the first 18 months: estimated taxes of 2,500,000 dollars, a placeholder only; process costs of 400,000 dollars across both countries; and 1,000,000 dollars of equity to keep one project in balance after the lender reduces the loan on losing the guarantor. Total need: 3,900,000 dollars.

What can it reach? The Country A account, 700,000 dollars, after about four months. The Country B account, 800,000 dollars, after about 13 months, once local authority is granted. The home is not for sale; the spouse lives there. The shares cannot be sold quickly at a fair price. Reachable within 18 months: 1,500,000 dollars. The liquidity gap is 2,400,000 dollars. Unless it is filled, the executor must sell project shares in a hurry, and a buyer who knows the seller is forced may pay 20 percent below fair value. On 3,000,000 dollars of shares, that discount is 600,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

The currency leak

Second worked example, hypothetical. The executor must move 2,000,000 dollars of value from Country B to pay tax and costs in Country A. A bank charges a spread of 1.5 percent on the conversion, 30,000 dollars. Suppose too that, during the 13 months the Country B funds were frozen, Country B's currency fell 10 percent against Country A's. The 2,000,000 dollars of value is now worth 1,800,000 dollars in Country A terms before the spread, and about 1,773,000 dollars after it. Neither leak is anybody's fault. Both are consequences of time and borders, and both grow with every month of delay.

Closing the gap

Each leak has a planning response, in concept. Frozen liquidity: hold some assets through structures that do not die, such as a company with a second signatory, and keep a reserve where your heirs can reach it. Process costs: coordinated wills, documents prepared in advance and an asset list cut months off. Triggered debt: negotiate with lenders now for a reasonable cure period and a replacement-guarantor mechanism. Forced sales: life insurance sized to the liquidity gap, owned in a way that keeps the proceeds available to the estate or the family, with a licensed adviser deciding the form. Currency: keep reserves in the currency where the obligations arise. Double tax: identify any treaty or relief and the documents needed to claim it.

Applied to the example, if insurance of 2,500,000 dollars were in place and reachable within three months, the forced-sale discount of 600,000 dollars would disappear, and most of the currency risk too.

Wealth Ledger

Add a line to your personal balance sheet called "estate liquidity gap", calculated as above, and update it annually. It is a contingent liability your family carries. If the gap is large, you are more exposed than your net worth suggests, because your wealth is in assets that cannot be reached when they are needed.

Family, legacy and what enough means

Here is a question for you, Mr Shabazz, not an answer. If your estate were settled tomorrow, what would you want it to make possible for the people you care about, and what would you not want it to do to them? Write your answer down before you read any estate plan.

The answer is yours to define. It may be a number, or a set of values, or both. What it is not is something an adviser can supply. Every structure this week is a means; your answer is the end it serves.

The incapacity version of the gap

Incapacity produces its own liquidity gap, and it can be worse, because there is no estate yet and no executor, only a person who cannot sign. Hypothetically, a developer suffers a stroke and is unable to manage his affairs for 18 months. His personal accounts in Country B need a Country B authority to operate. His companies need a director's signature for every draw request. His spouse needs income. If his power of attorney was drafted only for Country A, and the companies have no second signatory, the project may stop drawing, the lender may treat the inability to sign as a breach, and the family may need a court application in Country B to appoint someone. Each of those steps costs months. The remedy is the same toolkit applied earlier: a second signatory in each company, a power of attorney for each country tested with the institutions that must accept it, and a reserve the family can reach without his signature.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an estate that is wealthy on paper and illiquid in practice. The control is the annual liquidity gap calculation, with each leak priced and a named response for each.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is forgetting the loans. Many developers check their will and never read what their loan agreements say happens when a guarantor dies.

Callback

In the stress tests week, I asked you to model the severe case, not only the base case. Death and incapacity are the severe case for a family balance sheet. Run them the same way: shock, timeline, gap, response.

Recap

Six leaks: frozen liquidity, process costs, triggered debt, forced sales, currency and double tax. Compute the liquidity gap, price each leak, and close it with structure, documents, lender terms, insurance and reserves.

Next lesson: LEX, on the rules: which law governs which asset, multiple wills and incapacity documents.
checklist: I compute my estate liquidity gap for the first 18 months, at least annually.
I know which loans and guarantees treat my death or incapacity as a default or review trigger.
I have asked lenders for a cure period and a replacement-guarantor mechanism.
I keep a reserve my family can reach quickly, in the currency where obligations arise.
I hold key assets through structures with a second authorised signatory.
I have asked a licensed adviser whether insurance should cover the liquidity gap.
I have identified any double tax relief and the documents needed to claim it.
I have written my own answer to what my estate should make possible.
head: Field checklist
speak: An unplanned cross-border estate leaks value through six holes: frozen liquidity, process costs, triggered debt, forced sales, currency and double tax. Measure it as an estate liquidity gap: cash needed in the first 12 to 24 months minus cash actually reachable. Hypothetically, a 20,000,000 dollar estate needs 3,900,000 dollars in 18 months for placeholder taxes, costs and project equity, but can reach only 1,500,000 because one account is frozen for 13 months and the rest is in shares and a family home. The 2,400,000 gap forces hurried share sales, perhaps at a 20 percent discount. A 10 percent currency fall and a 1.5 percent spread cut another 227,000 dollars from 2,000,000 moved. The responses: structures that keep signing, coordinated documents, lender cure periods, reachable reserves in the right currency, insurance sized to the gap and treaty relief. A licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Estate liquidity gap — the difference between the cash an estate needs in its first months and the cash it can actually reach in that time.
Forced-sale discount — the price reduction a buyer demands when it knows the seller must sell quickly.
Replacement-guarantor mechanism — a loan term allowing a new guarantor to be substituted, within a set period, if the original dies or loses capacity.

hostile.q: Your loan has a 90-day clause on the death of the guarantor. If you die, how does your estate replace you in 90 days when probate in this country takes a year?
hostile.a: It cannot do that through probate, so I am not relying on it. I am asking you for two changes: a cure period long enough for my estate to act, and a named replacement guarantor, my holding company or a family member with sufficient net worth, who can step in by delivering a guarantee and financial statements. Separately, I hold life insurance sized to the equity this project would need if the loan were reduced, and I can show you the policy summary.

title: Which Law Governs Which Asset, and How Two Wills Can Cancel Each Other
summary: Cross-border estates are governed by conflict of laws rules that decide which country's law applies to each asset and to the will itself. The commonest drafting failure is one will revoking another. Incapacity documents raise a separate recognition problem. Learn the concepts before you instruct lawyers in two countries.
body:
Before a court decides who inherits, it decides whose law to use. Those choice-of-law rules, and the way wills in different countries interact, decide more cross-border estates than any clause about who gets what.

Recall

Q. What is an estate liquidity gap?

A. The difference between the cash an estate needs in its first months and the cash it can actually reach in that time.

Q. What is a deemed disposition?

A. A rule treating a person or trust as having sold an asset at market value on a defined event, such as death, without an actual sale.

Q. What is an indemnity in a contract?

A. A promise by one party to cover specified losses suffered by another, often regardless of fault, within limits the contract sets.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when you instruct an estates lawyer in each country, you are asking them to fit their documents into a puzzle whose pieces belong to different legal systems. If you understand the shape of the puzzle, you can make sure the pieces are cut to fit. This is concept teaching. These rules vary between countries, and within federal countries between provinces or states. Verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: an estates lawyer in each country where you hold property, instructed to coordinate with the others.

Conflict of laws, in plain words

Plain English. When a case touches more than one country, each country has rules about which country's law should decide each question. Lawyers call this conflict of laws, or private international law. It is not about conflict between people; it is about the choice between legal systems.

The professional framing for succession, in many common law systems, has traditionally run like this. Land and other immovable property passes under the law of the place where it lies. Movable property, such as bank accounts and shares, passes under the law of the deceased's domicile at death. Whether a will is formally valid, meaning properly signed and witnessed, may be judged under any of several laws, such as the law where it was made or the law of domicile, under rules designed to save wills from technical failure. Other systems, especially civil law ones, may apply a single law to the whole estate, and some allow a person to choose the law of their nationality. Some systems also protect certain family members with fixed shares, sometimes called forced heirship, which a will cannot override for property governed by that law.

Applied example, hypothetical. A person domiciled in Country A dies owning land in Country B. Under a traditional common law approach, Country B's law governs who inherits the land. If Country B gives a surviving spouse a fixed share of land regardless of the will, the will's gift of the whole parcel to a child may not fully take effect there. The child is surprised; the lawyer in Country B is not.

Say that out loud now.

Multiple wills and the revocation trap

Many cross-border families use two or more wills: one for each country's assets, each drafted to that country's formalities and process. Done well, this speeds probate because each executor deals with a local court using a local document.

The trap is the revocation clause. Most standard wills open with words to the effect of "I revoke all former wills". If the person signs a will in Country A covering everything, and later signs a will in Country B with a standard revocation clause, the Country B will may revoke the Country A will entirely. The result can be that Country A assets pass under intestacy, despite two valid-looking wills on file.

Second applied example, hypothetical. In year one, a developer signs a Country A will leaving everything to his spouse. In year five he buys land in Country B and signs a local will leaving the land to his spouse, using the Country B lawyer's standard form, which revokes all earlier wills. He dies in year six. Depending on how each country reads the clause, his Country A home and accounts may now pass under Country A's intestacy rules, which might split them between spouse and children. The fix is drafting each will to cover only assets in its own country and to revoke only earlier wills dealing with that country, and having each lawyer read the other's draft.

Recognition of grants and of incapacity documents

Probate authority from one country is not automatically accepted in another. Some countries reseal or recognise grants from listed countries, often Commonwealth ones; others require a separate application. Verify the procedure for each country.

Incapacity documents are harder. A power of attorney is a document in which a person authorises someone else to act for them, and for property it often needs to be specially drafted to continue after the person loses capacity. Formalities, names and scope differ widely. A power valid in Country A may be refused by a bank, a land registry or a company in Country B. Some international arrangements exist to help recognition between participating countries, but coverage is limited. The safest approach is usually a separate power drafted for each country, by a local lawyer, covering assets there, and checked with the institutions that will need to accept it.

Formalities, translation and the original

Three practical points decide whether a will that is valid in law actually works in practice. First, formalities: the number and type of witnesses, whether a witness may also be a beneficiary, and whether a notary is required differ between countries, and a will that fails a local formality may be refused in that country even if valid elsewhere. Second, translation: a court or registry may require a certified translation of a foreign will or grant, which takes time and cost. Third, the original: many courts want the signed original, not a copy, and a lost original can create a presumption that the will was revoked, depending on local law. So for each country, ask the local lawyer three questions: what formalities make a will acceptable here, what translation and certification will be needed, and where should the original be kept so the executor can produce it. Verify each answer against current local practice, because procedures change.

A short applied example, hypothetical. A Country B will is signed with one witness, which Country B accepts, but the executor needs to use it to support a sale of a Country A account, and Country A requires two witnesses for a will to be accepted on its own. The executor must then prove validity by a slower route. One extra witness on the day of signing would have avoided it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is two lawyers, each competent, producing documents that defeat each other. The control is a written coordination instruction: each lawyer is told about the other country, each will is limited to its own assets, each revocation clause is limited accordingly, and each lawyer reviews and confirms the other's draft before signing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is signing a new will in a new country without telling the lawyer about the old one. The lawyer cannot protect a document he does not know exists.

Callback

In the contract forms week, Marco and I taught that an order of precedence clause decides which document wins when two contract documents conflict. Coordinated wills need the same discipline: each must say which assets it covers and which earlier documents it leaves alone, or the later one may silently win.

Recap

Conflict of laws decides whose law governs each asset; land usually follows where it lies, movables often follow domicile, though systems differ and some protect fixed family shares. Multiple wills work only if each is limited to its country and revokes nothing else. Grants and powers of attorney need recognition, country by country.

Next lesson: Roman, reverse engineering the gross estate needed to deliver a net result to heirs.
checklist: I tell every estates lawyer about every asset and every will in other countries.
I ask which country's law will govern each of my assets and the validity of each will.
I check whether any country where I hold property gives family members fixed shares.
I ensure each will covers only its own country's assets.
I ensure each revocation clause is limited to earlier wills for that country.
I have each lawyer review the other's draft before signing.
I hold a separate power of attorney for each country, checked with the institutions that must accept it.
I confirm how each country recognises a foreign grant of probate.
head: Field checklist
speak: Before a court decides who inherits, it decides whose law applies. That is conflict of laws. In many common law systems, land passes under the law of where it lies, movables like accounts and shares under the law of domicile, and formal validity of a will can be judged under several laws to save it from technical failure. Civil law systems may apply one law to the whole estate, and some protect family members with fixed shares a will cannot override. Multiple wills, one per country, can speed probate, but a standard revocation clause in a later will can revoke the earlier one entirely, leaving assets to pass under intestacy. So limit each will to its own assets, limit each revocation clause, and have each lawyer review the other's draft. Probate grants and powers of attorney also need recognition country by country. Verify every rule against the primary source.
terms: Conflict of laws — the rules a court uses to decide which country's law governs a case that touches more than one country.
Revocation clause — the words in a will cancelling earlier wills, which can unintentionally cancel a will made for another country.
Power of attorney — a document authorising someone to act for a person, which for property may need special wording to continue after loss of capacity.

hostile.q: You have a will here and a will at home. How do I know the newer one did not revoke the older one?
hostile.a: Because each was drafted to prevent exactly that. The will here covers only assets in this country and revokes only earlier wills dealing with them. The home will covers everything else and expressly preserves this one. Each lawyer reviewed the other's draft and confirmed it in writing, and I can provide both letters along with the wills.

title: Reverse Engineering the Estate Behind a Promised Inheritance
summary: Start from the net amount a person wants each heir to receive and work backward through currency, forced-sale discounts, debt, process costs and tax to find the gross estate and the liquidity it requires. The method shows how much of a cross-border estate never reaches the family. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
The amount your heirs receive is what is left after every leak. Working backward from the number you want them to receive shows how large the estate must be, and how much liquidity it needs, to deliver it.

Recall

Q. What is the revocation trap in multiple wills?

A. A later will with a standard clause revoking all former wills can cancel an earlier will made for another country, leaving those assets to pass under intestacy.

Q. What is the present value of an annuity?

A. The lump sum today that, earning a given return, pays a fixed amount each year for a set period and is then exhausted.

Q. What does a limitation of liability clause do?

A. It caps the amount a party can be made to pay under a contract, often with exceptions, such as fraud, that the parties negotiate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, people describe estates by their gross value. Heirs experience the net. In a cross-border estate the gap between the two can be large and is mostly predictable. This lesson starts from the outcome and works back, layer by layer. All numbers are hypothetical round figures, and every tax and cost rate is a placeholder, not a fact about any country. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The finished outcome

A developer wants each of his two children to receive 3,000,000 dollars, in Country A currency, net of everything, so 6,000,000 dollars in total, received within two years of death. His assets are in Country B, in its currency, held as project company shares and some cash. The question: what must his gross estate be in Country B, and how much of it must be liquid?

Step one: currency

The children will receive money in Country A. Assume, hypothetically, a 1.5 percent conversion spread and a planning allowance for a 10 percent currency fall while the estate is administered. To deliver 6,000,000 dollars in Country A, the estate needs, before the spread, 6,000,000 divided by 0.985, about 6,091,000 dollars of value in Country A terms. To survive a 10 percent fall, it must hold value worth 6,091,000 divided by 0.90, about 6,768,000 dollars at today's exchange rate. Currency alone adds about 768,000 dollars.

Step two: process costs

Assume, hypothetically, legal, court, executor, valuation and translation costs in both countries of 3 percent of the gross estate. Hold that for a moment, because it depends on the gross figure, and we will solve for it at the end.

Step three: tax

Assume, as a placeholder only, that tax on death takes 20 percent of the value passing, and that relief removes any second layer of tax. In reality, a system might tax accrued gains rather than total value, or tax heirs, or impose nothing; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Under the placeholder, the net value after tax and after process costs must equal 6,768,000 dollars. If tax is 20 percent and costs are 3 percent of gross, the estate keeps 77 percent of gross. Gross must be 6,768,000 divided by 0.77, about 8,790,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Step four: debt and the forced sale

Now the practical leaks. Suppose the estate must repay 1,000,000 dollars of personal debt, including a guarantee called after the death, from the gross estate. Add it: the gross needed rises to about 9,790,000 dollars, treating the debt as paid before tax for simplicity in this placeholder model.

Then liquidity. Of that estate, how much must be cash within two years? Tax of about 1,758,000 dollars (20 percent of 8,790,000), costs of about 264,000 dollars, debt of 1,000,000 dollars and the children's 6,000,000 dollars equivalent, which is 6,768,000 dollars before currency, all need cash. If the estate's own cash is only 1,500,000 dollars, the rest must come from selling shares. Suppose a forced-sale discount of 20 percent. To raise 1 dollar of cash, the executor must sell shares worth 1.25 dollars of fair value. If the estate must raise about 8,290,000 dollars from shares, the shares sold must be worth about 10,360,000 dollars at fair value. The discount alone costs about 2,070,000 dollars, pushing the required gross estate close to 11,860,000 dollars.

LayerRunning requirement
Net to heirs, Country A6,000,000 dollars
After currency spread and 10 percent fall allowanceabout 6,768,000 dollars
Grossed up for placeholder tax and costsabout 8,790,000 dollars
Plus personal debtabout 9,790,000 dollars
Plus forced-sale discountabout 11,860,000 dollars

To deliver 6,000,000 dollars, this estate needs roughly 11,860,000 dollars on these assumptions. Almost half never reaches the family.

Step five: which leaks can be closed

A second worked example, changing two inputs. Suppose the developer holds a reserve and insurance so that no forced sale is needed, and keeps part of the reserve in Country A currency so only half the transfer is exposed to the currency fall. Without the forced-sale discount, the requirement falls to about 9,790,000 dollars. Halving the currency exposure reduces the Country A-equivalent need from 6,768,000 to about 6,430,000 dollars, which grosses up to about 8,350,000 dollars, and with debt about 9,350,000 dollars. Two planning steps, with no change to tax law, reduce the gross estate required by about 2,500,000 dollars. Tax is the leak most people focus on; here, the larger avoidable leaks were liquidity and currency.

Step six: run the same method for incapacity

The reverse method also works for incapacity, where the promise is not an inheritance but a monthly income for a spouse while the developer cannot act. Suppose, hypothetically, the spouse needs 15,000 dollars a month in Country A for up to 24 months, a total of 360,000 dollars, and the family's only reachable cash is in a Country B account that will be inaccessible for at least 12 months without a Country B authority. The first 12 months, 180,000 dollars, must therefore be held in Country A, in a form the spouse can reach in her own name or through a power of attorney valid there. With a 10 percent currency fall allowance on any funds that must move later, the second 12 months need about 200,000 dollars of Country B value. The method is identical: state the outcome, list the leaks in order, gross up for each, and separate what must be liquid from what is merely valuable. The difference is that incapacity plans must work while the person is alive and unable to sign, which is why the documents and the reserve must be in place before anything happens.

Notice what the incapacity case adds to the inheritance case. The inheritance calculation asks how large the estate must be. The incapacity calculation asks where the money must already be sitting, in whose name, and under which country's authority, on the day the person stops being able to sign. Two estates of identical value can give completely different answers to that second question, and only the second question decides whether the family can pay its bills next month.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is promising heirs a number based on gross value. The control is a reverse calculation, from the net promise back to gross, updated annually, with the liquidity requirement shown separately from the value.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is ignoring the order of operations. Costs and tax depend on the gross estate, discounts depend on how much must be sold, and currency depends on where obligations arise. Work the layers in order, and check that each depends on the right base.

Callback

In the trusts week, Nadia worked backward from a promised yearly payment to the fund needed. This is the same method applied to a one-time promise, with more leaks, and it carries the same lesson: price the promise in capital before you make it.

Recap

Start with the net promise. Gross it up for currency, tax and costs, add debt, then add the forced-sale discount on whatever must be sold. Then close the avoidable leaks with reserves, insurance and currency matching, and recompute.

Next lesson: LEX, in the room with lawyers from two countries.
checklist: I state the net amount I want each heir to receive, in their currency and by when.
I gross it up for conversion spread and a currency fall allowance.
I gross up for tax and process costs using the right base, with placeholder rates checked by an adviser.
I add personal debt and any guarantee that could be called.
I compute how much must be sold and the forced-sale discount on it.
I show liquidity required separately from value.
I test reserves, insurance and currency matching to close leaks.
I update the reverse calculation every year.
head: Field checklist
speak: Heirs receive what is left after every leak, so work backward. Hypothetically, a developer wants his two children to receive 3,000,000 dollars each, 6,000,000 in total, in Country A, from assets held in Country B. A 1.5 percent spread and a 10 percent currency fall allowance raise that to about 6,768,000. Grossing up for a placeholder 20 percent tax and 3 percent process costs gives about 8,790,000. Add 1,000,000 of personal debt: about 9,790,000. If most of the cash must come from selling shares at a 20 percent forced-sale discount, the requirement rises to about 11,860,000. Almost half never reaches the family. Reserves and insurance that remove the forced sale, and holding part of the reserve in the heirs' currency, cut the requirement by about 2,500,000 dollars without any change to tax. Show liquidity separately from value, and update every year. A licensed adviser is required before you act.
terms: Gross estate — the total value of a person's property at death before debts, costs and taxes.
Net to heirs — what beneficiaries actually receive after every cost, tax, discount and conversion.
Currency fall allowance — a planning margin that assumes a currency may weaken during administration, to protect a promised amount.

hostile.q: You told your children they will each inherit 3,000,000 dollars. Your estate is worth 9,000,000. Why is that not enough?
hostile.a: Because 9,000,000 is gross value in another currency, mostly in shares. On placeholder assumptions, after currency, tax, costs, debt and a forced-sale discount, it delivers well under 6,000,000 dollars. So I am either lowering the promise or closing the leaks: a reachable reserve, insurance sized to the liquidity gap, and part of the reserve held in their currency. I would rather show them the arithmetic now than leave them to discover it.

title: The Meeting That Makes Two Lawyers Work as One
summary: A realistic scene: Mr Shabazz convenes his estates lawyer at home and a lawyer in a second country on a video call to coordinate wills and incapacity documents. Learn how to set the agenda, what to say, what never to say, the question behind each lawyer's caution, and how to leave with one plan.
body:
Two good lawyers who never speak to each other can produce two good documents that defeat each other. The meeting that prevents this is yours to run, because you are the only person who sees both countries.

Recall

Q. In a reverse estate calculation, which avoidable leaks are often larger than tax?

A. Liquidity and currency: forced-sale discounts and conversion losses, which reserves, insurance and currency matching can reduce.

Q. What should you say when asked to become a trustee?

A. That you are honoured, that your duty would be to all beneficiaries and the deed, and that you need to see the deed and take advice before deciding.

Q. In a dispute, why is mediation often tried before arbitration or court?

A. Because it is cheaper and faster, keeps control of the outcome with the parties, and can preserve relationships; it produces a binding result only if the parties sign a settlement.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every cross-border estate plan eventually depends on one meeting where the lawyers align. It is often skipped because it feels expensive. It is the cheapest meeting in the whole plan. The scene below is hypothetical; the lawyers, countries and numbers are invented for teaching.

The scene

You have asked your estates lawyer in Country A, whom we will call Ms Ortiz, to join a video call with a lawyer in Country B, Mr Baptiste. You hold a home and investments in Country A and two parcels and a project company in Country B. You sent both lawyers, a week earlier, a one-page asset list by country and a short note of what you want: your spouse secure, your children treated equally, the project able to keep signing if you die or lose capacity.

Setting the agenda

Open with the agenda, aloud: "Thank you both. I have three goals for this hour. First, agree which document governs each asset on my list. Second, make sure neither will revokes the other. Third, agree what happens if I lose capacity, in each country. At the end I would like a single written note of who drafts what and by when."

Say that out loud now.

The lines to say

To both: "Please each tell me what you need from the other to make your document safe." Then let them talk to each other. Your role is to keep them talking about the same list.

When Mr Baptiste raises a local rule, for example a protected share for a spouse in Country B land: "Thank you. Ms Ortiz, does that change anything in your will for Country A, so the two together still treat my children equally?"

When the conversation drifts to tax: "That is important and I will take it to our tax advisers in both countries. For today, can we note it as an open item and keep to the wills and incapacity documents?"

Before closing: "So, each will covers only its own country's assets, each revocation clause is limited to its own country, and each of you will review the other's draft before I sign. Ms Ortiz will circulate the note by Friday. Is that right?"

The question behind each lawyer's caution

When Ms Ortiz says "I cannot advise on Country B law", her real concern is professional liability; she will not stand behind advice outside her qualification. That is correct and it protects you. The answer is not to push her, but to ask Mr Baptiste the question and have her confirm only the effect on her document.

When Mr Baptiste says "Our standard form revokes all prior wills", his real concern is certainty; local courts like a clean slate. The answer is to ask him to tailor the clause and to record why in the note.

The lines never to say

Never say "Just use one will for everything, it is simpler." It may be simpler to sign and much harder to probate, and it may not work for land in another country.

Never say "Can you two just work it out between you?" and leave. Without the client, neither lawyer knows the family's priorities, and each will default to protecting their own document.

Never ask one lawyer to give an opinion on the other's country's law. You will either get a refusal or an opinion nobody should rely on.

When to stay silent

Stay silent when the two lawyers start talking to each other directly about a technical point. That is the meeting working. Interrupt only to bring them back to the asset list or to ask, "What does that mean for my family?"

A worked example in the room

Hypothetically, Mr Baptiste says local probate in Country B for an estate of your size typically takes 9 to 15 months. You ask: "If I hold the project company shares through a Country A holding company instead of personally, would Country B probate still be needed for them?" He answers that if you do not personally own the Country B shares, they are not part of your Country B estate, though the parcels you own personally still are. Ms Ortiz notes that the holding company shares would then pass under her will in Country A. That one question may remove the largest asset from a slow process. You note it as an option to cost with your tax advisers, because moving shares into a holding company may itself be a taxable event.

How the best do it

Families with complex cross-border estates often appoint a lead adviser who maintains the master asset list and coordinates the local lawyers, holds a joint review whenever an asset or residence changes, and keeps a single memorandum recording which document governs each asset. You can copy that with one lawyer as lead, an annual call and a one-page memorandum.

Holding your state

Talking about your own death or incapacity is uncomfortable, and the discomfort can make you rush. Slow down. Treat it as a design review of a structure you care about. The calmer you are, the more precisely the lawyers will work.

After the meeting

Within a week of the call, check three things. Has the note arrived, and does it match what was agreed? Has each lawyer received the other's draft, with a date for comments? And has every open item, such as the tax question about the holding company, been sent to the right adviser with a deadline? A coordination meeting decays quickly if nobody owns the follow-up, and the owner is you. Put a date in your calendar 12 months out for the joint review, and another for any change in residence, marriage or a major purchase.

Finally, tell your executor and your coordinator, in one short letter, where the note and the originals are kept and who the two lawyers are, so the plan survives even if you are not there to explain it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is leaving the meeting with goodwill and no written allocation of tasks. The control is the closing summary and a dated note that lists each document, its author, its scope and the cross-review step.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is not sending the asset list in advance. Lawyers who meet the facts for the first time on the call spend the hour discovering them. Professional sign-off required: an estates lawyer in each country.

Callback

In the using professionals week, LEX and Vera taught that clear instructions and a written engagement letter decide the quality of advice. This meeting is a joint instruction. The asset list and the written note are what make two engagements behave like one.

Recap

Send the asset list in advance, open with three goals, let the lawyers talk to each other, park tax, never ask one to opine on the other's law, and close with a written note of who drafts what, each will limited to its country, and cross-review before signing.

Next lesson: Kema, with six questions, Cole's Auditor's Chair and a boardroom drill on cross-border estates.
checklist: I send both lawyers a one-page asset list by country and my goals a week before the meeting.
I open with no more than three goals and a request for a written note.
I let the lawyers speak to each other and keep them on the asset list.
I never ask one lawyer to advise on the other country's law.
I park tax questions for tax advisers in both countries.
I confirm each will covers only its own assets with a limited revocation clause.
I agree cross-review of drafts before anything is signed.
I leave with a dated note of each document, author, scope and deadline.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two good lawyers who never speak can produce two documents that defeat each other, so you run the meeting that aligns them. Hypothetically, you hold assets in Country A and Country B. A week ahead, send both lawyers a one-page asset list and your goals. Open with three: agree which document governs each asset, ensure neither will revokes the other, and agree incapacity arrangements in each country. Let them talk to each other and keep them on the list. Park tax for tax advisers. When one lawyer says she cannot advise on the other's law, that protects you; ask the other lawyer. Never ask for one will for everything, never leave them to sort it out alone, and never ask for an opinion outside a lawyer's qualification. A good question, like whether holding shares through a home-country company avoids foreign probate, can remove the largest asset from a slow process. Close with a written note of who drafts what, and when.
terms: Ancillary probate — a separate grant of authority obtained in a second country to deal with assets there.
Resealing — a procedure in some countries that recognises a grant of probate made in another listed country.
Lead adviser — the professional who keeps the master asset list and coordinates advisers across countries.

hostile.q: Your Country B lawyer and your Country A lawyer disagree on whether the spouse's protected share applies to the project company shares. Which of them do I believe?
hostile.a: Neither alone. The question is which country's law governs those shares, and that depends partly on how they are held. I have asked both lawyers to set out their reasoning in writing and to speak to each other directly. If they still disagree, I will either restructure the holding so the answer is clear, or obtain a formal opinion from a specialist in the governing law before relying on either view.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 92 Review: Cross-Border Estates and Cole's Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions test domicile, situs, probate, the Hughes estate, liquidity leaks, conflict of laws and coordinated wills. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a hypothetical estate summary as a hostile auditor would. A boardroom drill explains a cross-border estate plan in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a life lived across borders leaves several estates, and a plan works only if every country's documents, authority and cash are lined up before they are needed.

Recall

Q. Why should you send lawyers an asset list before a coordination meeting?

A. So they arrive knowing the facts and spend the hour solving the plan rather than discovering what you own.

Q. What does an estate freeze move?

A. Future growth, and the latent tax on it, from the founder's fixed-value shares to growth shares, often held by a trust.

Q. What is a hostile auditor looking for in a document?

A. Claims without evidence, internal contradictions, missing authority, undisclosed conflicts and anything that would not survive an independent check.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions without notes, you can lead your own cross-border estate plan rather than wait for advisers to discover it. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are domicile and situs, and why do they matter?

Answer: Domicile is the country a person treats as a permanent home; situs is where the law treats an asset as located. In many common law systems, land passes under the law of where it lies and most movables under the law of domicile, so the two facts decide which law governs which asset.

Question 2. Why can assets freeze after death in a second country?

Answer: Because probate authority from one country is not automatically recognised in another. Until local authority is granted, by resealing or ancillary probate, banks, registries and companies may refuse to act.

Question 3. State Rule 92 and the case behind it.

Answer: Never let your estate depend on what a court decides you intended: record your home, keep coordinated, findable wills for each country and incapacity documents each country will accept. Howard Hughes died in 1976 with no proved will, a contested domicile and years of litigation.

Question 4. Name the six leaks of a cross-border estate.

Answer: Frozen liquidity, process costs, triggered debt, forced sales, currency, and double tax.

Question 5. What is the revocation trap?

Answer: A later will with a standard clause revoking all former wills can cancel an earlier will made for another country. Each will should cover only its own assets and revoke only earlier wills for that country.

Question 6. Why is incapacity often harder to plan for than death across borders?

Answer: Because there is no clear trigger, and powers of attorney are creatures of local law, so one made in one country may be refused in another. A separate power for each country, checked with the institutions that must accept it, is usually safer.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Tessa and LEX framed the cross-border estate as several estates with their own courts. Ford and Cole took the Howard Hughes estate through seven steps and gave Rule 92. Roman priced the six leaks and the estate liquidity gap. LEX taught conflict of laws, multiple wills and recognition of grants and powers. Roman reverse engineered the gross estate behind a net promise. LEX ran the meeting that made two lawyers work as one.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 92 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair. Read this hypothetical estate summary as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Estate Plan Summary, prepared by the client. 1. Domicile: Country A, since I am a citizen there. 2. Will: signed in Country A in year one, covers all worldwide assets. 3. Country B will: signed in year six using the local lawyer's standard form. 4. Powers of attorney: one general power signed in Country A, valid everywhere. 5. Liquidity: estate worth 14,000,000 dollars, so no liquidity concern. 6. Project loans: lender will understand if anything happens. 7. Originals: in my office safe; nobody else has the combination.

The defects. First, item 1 confuses citizenship with domicile; they are different tests and may point to different countries, so the claim needs evidence of permanent home. Second, items 2 and 3 together are the revocation trap: a standard Country B form likely revokes the worldwide Country A will, so the Country A assets may pass under intestacy. Third, item 4 assumes a power of attorney is valid everywhere, when recognition is country by country, and a general power may not survive loss of capacity unless drafted to. Fourth, item 5 confuses value with liquidity; no liquidity gap has been calculated. Fifth, item 6 is an assumption with no evidence; the loan agreements must be read for death and incapacity triggers. Sixth, item 7 makes the wills unfindable, which is the Hughes failure in miniature. Seventh, the document is prepared by the client alone, with no lawyer's confirmation in either country, so none of its claims are verified.

Common confusions

Four confusions recur this week. First, "I am a citizen, so that is my domicile". Citizenship, tax residence and domicile are different tests. Second, "my will covers my worldwide assets, so I am done". A single will may not work smoothly for land in another country and may be revoked by a later local will. Third, "my estate is large, so there is no cash problem". Value is not liquidity, and frozen accounts and forced sales are where cross-border estates lose the most. Fourth, "my power of attorney works everywhere". Recognition is country by country, and a power may not survive loss of capacity unless it is drafted to. If you hear any of these in a meeting, ask the lawyer for the rule, in writing, for each country.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a plan that looks complete on one page and fails at the first border. The control is an annual joint review: asset list by country, document for each, cross-review of wills, incapacity documents tested with institutions, liquidity gap recomputed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner's mistake is believing an estate plan is a single document. It is a coordinated set of documents, records and cash arrangements, one for each country, maintained over time.

Boardroom drill

Explain your cross-border estate plan in two minutes to a lender who has asked what happens to its loan if you die. Then read the model answer.

Model answer: "I hold assets in two countries, so I have planned for two estates. I have a will in each, each limited to its own country's assets and each reviewed by the other country's lawyer so neither revokes the other. My shares in the borrower are held through a holding company, which has a second authorised signatory, so the borrower keeps signing while my estate is administered. I have a power of attorney drafted for each country in case I lose capacity. I have calculated the cash my estate would need in its first 18 months, and I hold life insurance and a reserve to cover the gap, including the equity this loan would need if you reduced it. I am asking for a cure period and a replacement-guarantor mechanism in the loan, and my lawyer will give you a letter setting out how authority passes."

Callback

In the integrity week, REGA and Cole taught that beneficial ownership must be visible and consistent. An estate plan is the same discipline extended to the moment of death: the people who will own and control your assets must be identifiable, authorised and consistent across every country's records.

Recap

Domicile and situs pick the law; probate and powers of attorney give authority country by country; coordinated wills avoid the revocation trap; the liquidity plan stops the leaks; and records that can be found turn intention into evidence.

Why can assets freeze after death in a second country?
State Rule 92 and the case behind it.
Name the six leaks of a cross-border estate.
What is the revocation trap?
Why is incapacity often harder to plan for than death across borders?
head: The six questions
speak: This week, cross-border estates. A life across borders leaves several estates. Domicile, your permanent home, and situs, where each asset is located, decide which law governs which asset. Probate gives authority to act, but one country's grant is not automatically recognised in another, so assets can freeze. Howard Hughes died in 1976 with no proved will and a contested domicile, which gave Rule 92: record your home, keep coordinated, findable wills for each country and incapacity documents each will accept. An estate leaks through frozen liquidity, process costs, triggered debt, forced sales, currency and double tax, so compute the liquidity gap and close it. Multiple wills must each cover only their own assets, or a later one may revoke an earlier one. Powers of attorney need recognition country by country. Run the coordination meeting yourself, with an asset list, and review every year.
terms: Forced heirship — a rule in some legal systems giving certain family members a fixed share of an estate that a will cannot override.
Joint review — an annual meeting of advisers from each country to confirm that documents, assets and records still fit together.
Second authorised signatory — a person other than the owner empowered to sign for a company, so it can act if the owner dies or loses capacity.

hostile.q: Your summary says your domicile is Country A because you are a citizen. You spend most of the year in Country B. Why should a tax authority accept that?
hostile.a: It should not accept it on citizenship alone, and I have corrected that line. Domicile is about where I treat as my permanent home, and I have asked my lawyers in both countries to assess it on the facts: where my family home is, where I intend to return, my ties in each place. I keep a written record of those facts, and my wills and tax filings will be consistent with whatever the advice concludes.
